extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers interested in rhetorical technique, persuasive prose, and use of paradox (esp. those studying Chestertonian style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing persuasive, literary prose that uses paradox, vivid analogy, and the deliberate juxtaposition of opposites to reveal deeper truths. Applicable to essayists and creative nonfiction writers aiming for dramatic moral argument and rhetorical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual insight is tested by guessing hidden malformations or surprises
rubrics_metrics.description: "Actual insight or inspiration is best tested by whether it guesses these hidden malformations or surprises.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the 'mathematician from the moon' who sees obvious symmetry but only a deeper observer would guess the heart's true place; in prose, genuine insight is shown when an account 'suddenly becomes illogical' at precisely the points reality is illogical. Anti-pattern: merely cataloguing obvious facts (arms, ears) without perceiving the deeper irregularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a doctrine 'goes wrong' exactly where reality goes wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not merely that it deduces logical truths, but that when it suddenly becomes illogical, it has found, so to speak, an illogical truth.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deliberate, apparent violations of logic or conventional consistency to signal a deeper, paradoxical truth—i.e., craft moments that seem to 'go wrong' so they resonate with real-world irregularities. Example: Christianity's apparent illogicalities match human experience of contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication (convergence of reasons) as evidence of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more complicated seems the coincidence, the less it can be a coincidence.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that complex, converging proofs or elaborate doctrines increase credibility; treat intricate detail and doctrinal elaboration as a compliment. Analogy: if a key fits a lock (complex match) it's more reliable than a stick fitting a hole by accident. Writing guidance: accumulate diverse, converging examples rather than rely on a single neat proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conviction grows from many converging reasons and resists sudden summation
rubrics_metrics.description: "A man is not really convinced of a philosophic theory when he finds that something proves it. He is only really convinced when he finds that everything proves it... the more bewildered he is if asked suddenly to sum them up.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing persuasive prose, recognize and convey that deep belief often rests on a multiplicity of impressions; avoid forcing a single compact summary when the strength lies in cumulative, diverse evidence. Use catalogues of varied instances to simulate that conviction; accept that immediate summary may feel helpless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contradictions and self-contradictory criticisms as a test for centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was attacked on all sides and for all contradictory reasons... This puzzled me; the charges seemed inconsistent.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an idea is attacked equally for opposite vices, consider presenting that as an index of the idea's centrality or normalcy. Rhetorical strategy: compile seemingly contradictory criticisms to suggest the target is the 'centre' that polarises critics in different directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain critics by examining their biases (critic-as-key-to-criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I tested this idea by asking myself whether there was about any of the accusers anything morbid that might explain the accusation.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In polemic or persuasive writing, attribute particular criticisms to corresponding psychological or social dispositions of critics (e.g., Swinburne's hedonism explains some attacks). Use this to neutralize or reinterpret objections. Anti-pattern: treating all criticisms as equally objective without considering the critic's standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep opposites side by side rather than blend them—separate then exaggerate both
rubrics_metrics.description: "It separated the two ideas and then exaggerated them both.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: to preserve the power of opposing qualities (e.g., pride and humility, wrath and love), present them as distinct extremes and allow each to be full-strength rather than diluting both into a tame compromise. Examples: Christianity's exaltation of man and abjection of man simultaneously; charity made both more wrathful about crime and more tender to criminals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer conflict (duplex passion) over balance (meson) for moral texture
rubrics_metrics.description: "Paganism declared that virtue was in a balance; Christianity declared it was in a conflict: the collision of two passions apparently opposite.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose moral argument around dynamic tensions and dramatic collisions rather than mild equilibria. Use paradoxical pairings (e.g., desire to live + readiness to die for courage) to create richer ethical insight. Anti-pattern: presenting virtue as mere moderate compromise that loses intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete analogies and vivid, often whimsical examples to test or explain ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in text: mathematician from the moon, snowflakes forming maze at Hampton Court, key and lock, turnip or taximeter cab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ striking concrete analogies and surprising comparisons to render abstract claims palpable and test the subtlety of an insight. Such images both clarify and dramatize arguments. Avoid over-abstracting or relying solely on abstractions without vivid anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix a governing doctrine or definition to permit extreme expressions within limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "By defining its main doctrine, the Church not only kept seemingly inconsistent things side by side, but... allowed them to break out in a sort of artistic violence.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear central premise or framework so that strong, even extreme, rhetorical expressions don't dissolve into incoherence. A defined anchor lets you permit grandiose or severe statements (meekness as dramatic, fury as martyrdom) while maintaining overall coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ heroic/theatrical manner in moral writing to restore vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Historic Christianity rose into a high and strange COUP DE THEATRE of morality... Poetry could be acted as well as composed.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grand, theatrical diction, dramatic scenes, and monumental gestures to make moral claims memorable and powerful—restore spectacle where modern discourse tends to be timid. Example: saintly pity kissing a criminal's head. Anti-pattern: excessively muted, purely bureaucratic moral prose that loses imaginative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve purity of opposing qualities rather than create muddy compromises ('coexistent but pure')
rubrics_metrics.description: "keep two colours coexistent but pure... It is not a mixture like russet or purple; it is rather like a shot silk...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When juxtaposing opposites, ensure each retains its distinctiveness (like different warp and weft threads producing shifting colours) rather than blending into an indistinct gray. In practice, let opposing claims both speak strongly and visibly rather than averaging them into dull moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental and emotional liberty require structure; anarchy paralyzes feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mental and emotional liberty are not so simple as they look. Really they require almost as careful a balance of laws and conditions as do social and political liberty.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative or argumentative writing about freedom of feeling, show that constraints and definitions enable intense, recoverable emotion; pure refusal of all limits often produces numbness or incoherence. Use this to justify formal or doctrinal frames that enable rather than restrict expressive range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paradoxical virtue-definitions (e.g., courage, charity) as analytic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed paradoxes: courage = 'a strong desire to live taking the form of a readiness to die'; charity = 'divide the crime from the criminal... forgive the criminal unto seventy times seven while not forgiving the crime.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame virtues in paradoxical formulations to illuminate their complexity and to distinguish close but distinct ideas (hero vs suicide; criminal vs crime). Such formulations function as analytical tools and memorable lines for readers to grasp moral nuance.
